e: AWS DataSync transfers data online from on premises to S3 and automatically verifies the integrity of the transferred data (checksums) after the transfer. Snowball Edge is an offline device, S3 File Gateway and Transfer Acceleration don't provide built-in post-transfer integrity validation in the same way.

Route 53 is a highly available, fully managed DNS service, so creating hosted zones and importing the zone files removes all server management. EC2-based or migrated DNS servers keep the operational burden and are less available.

S3 Storage Lens gives organization-wide visibility across accounts and Regions, including metrics for incomplete multipart upload bytes and object counts, with no custom setup. Config, SCPs, and Multi-Region Access Points don't report that metric.

RDS Blue/Green Deployments create a synchronized staging copy of the production database so you can upgrade the version and test it, then switch over quickly with no data loss and minimal operational work. Snapshots, native restore, or DMS take more effort and risk.

The job takes up to 2 hours, which exceeds Lambda's 15-minute limit, and it can't resume if interrupted, so a Fargate task launched by an EventBridge schedule runs it on demand and bills only while running. A Reserved EC2 instance or ECS on EC2 pays for idle time.

Amazon Neptune is a managed graph database suited to relationships between users and interactions (recommendations), and Neptune Streams captures changes in the graph for monitoring, all managed. QLDB is a ledger database, and Kinesis Data Streams isn't Neptune's native change feed.

EFS is a shared file system that Linux instances across multiple AZs can mount and modify concurrently, and it grows automatically as the data grows. Glacier is archival, and a regular EBS volume can't be shared across AZs.

Database queries are the bottleneck, so a read replica offloads read traffic from the source instance. The Multi-AZ standby can't serve reads, Transfer Acceleration is an S3 feature, and Firehose doesn't increase database concurrency.

Cross-account access (bucket policy and IAM roles in the agencies' accounts) lets each agency's analysts read the data securely without copying or creating users, and it's easy to manage. S3 global tables don't exist, public buckets are insecure, and per-analyst IAM users are hard to manage.

Creating an FSx for ONTAP file system in the secondary Region and using NetApp SnapMirror for replication gives native, incremental DR replication that keeps the same CIFS and NFS access, with the least overhead. S3 or EFS copies change the protocols, and backup restores are slower.

Subscribing an SQS queue to the SNS topic and triggering Lambda from the queue buffers events so processing scales and no events are lost during spikes. ECS, EKS, or SMS aren't event-processing targets for this pattern.

Lambda scales from zero to hundreds of requests per second instantly and charges only for use, and DynamoDB handles unpredictable growth and simple key-value queries with on-demand scaling. Fargate, EC2 Auto Scaling, and Aurora are less suited to sudden scaling from zero.

A Lambda function that generates S3 presigned URLs lets employees anywhere securely upload or download specific objects with temporary access, with no servers or user management. IAM users per employee, file gateways, or SFTP with Secrets Manager require more administration.

Sticky sessions pin each client to one target, so traffic favors a single instance. Disabling session affinity lets the ALB distribute requests across all healthy instances evenly. NLB, more instances, or health check changes don't address the skew.

The Lambda function's execution role needs the kms:Decrypt permission (an IAM role attached to the function), and the KMS key policy must allow that role to decrypt. Resource policies and function-attached policies don't grant the function's outbound permissions.

Enable Cost and Usage Reports in the management account (covering all member accounts), deliver them to S3, and query monthly with Athena (pay per query), which is scalable and cheap. Kinesis, EMR, or Redshift add continuous cost or complexity for a monthly query.

A Network Load Balancer supports UDP and integrates with Auto Scaling groups, distributing game traffic across instances as the group scales. ALBs don't support UDP, and Route 53 weighted records or NAT instances don't scale properly.
Store the logs in S3 (cheap, scalable) and use Athena to run standard SQL on demand, paying only for queries run once a week. RDS, OpenSearch, or EMR clusters cost more to keep running.

Request a public ACM certificate for the apex domain and a wildcard for *.example.com to cover all country subdomains on the ALB, and validate ownership with DNS records (which also allows automatic renewal). Private certificates aren't for public websites, and email validation is manual.

An AWS KMS external key store (XKS) lets KMS use keys held in an external key manager outside AWS, supporting multiple vendors, with the least operational overhead. CloudHSM key stores keep keys in AWS, and the default key store keeps keys in AWS.

FSx for Lustre provides a high-performance parallel file system with sub-millisecond latency for HPC across hundreds of instances, and linking it to an S3 bucket lets engineers post-process the results from S3. EFS has higher latency, and S3 can't be mounted as a shared file system.

Global Accelerator gives static anycast IP addresses, routes users to the nearest healthy endpoint with health checks and automatic cross-Region failover, and doesn't rely on DNS or client IP caching. Route 53 or CloudFront depend on DNS caching or don't suit VoIP, and an ALB is regional.

FSx for Lustre persistent file systems provide high availability and replicated data with sub-millisecond latency and high sustained throughput for thousands of instances. Scratch file systems aren't replicated (not highly available), and EFS has higher latency.

gp3 storage for RDS lets you provision IOPS independently of storage capacity (up to 15,000+ IOPS on larger volumes), cheaper than io1. gp2 ties IOPS to storage size, io1 costs more, and magnetic is slow.

RDS for SQL Server is managed and supports read replicas (Enterprise edition) for reporting, with the least operational overhead and no application rewrite. SQL Server on EC2 keeps administration, and DynamoDB or Aurora MySQL aren't compatible with SQL Server.
